newsitem.title: UK: Europe grains market focuses on harvesting.
newsitem.headline: Europe grains market focuses on harvesting.

text.p: Most Western European grains markets concentrated on the harvest this week, as farmers in the north rushed to get the first of the new crop in, while rain frustrated those in Spain and Italy.
But the level of trading activity was limited, as market players awaited more definite signs on yields and quality. In the UK currency woes stifled the market.
Favourable crop weather and harvest progress ruled the French markets, dealers said.
Dry weather returned to France last weekend allowing farmers to begin the barley harvest and make the first cuts of soft wheat.
French new-crop wheat prices were broadly stable as initial reports from the fields eased fears wet conditions in June might hit grain quality north of the Loire river.
But trade was slack, with buyers and sellers still reluctant to make a move before the harvest is in full swing.
"Everyone looked at the fields this week and quality was the main focus. But the first cuts eased concern over crop quality north of the Loire river," one dealer said.
Next week may herald some trade action as the wheat harvest really gets going, he said.

The first cuts made north of the Loire river showed quality was "good" for barley and "satisfactory" for wheat but farmers in Poitou-Charentes, in France's centre-west, said high moisture levels caused unwanted grain germination, which could hit wheat quality.
With fears over crop quality receding operators focused on the size of the new harvest. "We may be heading for a new record crop," one dealer said.

France's grain office ONIC predicted another strong wheat crop this year of 34.01 million against the 1996's record 34.7 million tonnes as higher sowings partly offset a decline in yields following a prolonged spring drought.
Life for British traders has been made very difficult by the strength of sterling, and the widespread view that rising interest rates will send the currency higher.
"It kills the market stone dead," one trader, involved in exports, said.
Volume on the futures and the domestic market has gone down to low levels. "If you don't have to do anything, it's best to stay away," the trader said.
Sterling went over 2.99 marks to set a six year high on Friday, after an interest rate rise on Thursday.

The barley harvest got underway in the south, with fine weather for most of the week, although there were some showers. Analysts voiced concern over initial quality, but noted that the quality of first cuts is always poor.

German new crop wheat prices are narrowly steady from levels earlier this week when the first half September fob price for 12 percent protein was at 270 marks/tonne, down 20 from last year, with higher quality priced up to 310.
But favourable harvest weather in Europe was expected to weigh on prices ahead of the wheat harvest in August/September.
Barley markets were also quiet, with the old crop finished and harvesting about to start in the south west.
Traders said ex-harvest prices of 237.50 marks a tonne free Hamburg had traded earlier this week but buyers were now offering five marks less.
But the EU was seen more likely to offer rebates at its next weekly export tender next Thursday to enable exporters to supply Saudi Arabia and this could lift prices.
In Spain, harvesting has been completed in the south, but continued wet weather in the north is still causing delays.
New maize is not ready yet, and is thought likely to be later this year than last.
Durum wheat from the south is of variable quality, but overall poor, dealers said.
Some quality durum is available, but prices are higher at around 30,000 pesetas, they added.
Italian durum wheat prices were largely unchanged from first quotations last week and the Italian Institute for Agriculture Studies noted that the quality of the product is being evaluated.

The soft wheat harvest was delayed because of heavy rains particularly in northern Italy and Ismea noted that they may have to revise downwards production estimates and that the weather may have damaged the quality of the crop.
Maize prices are the lowest in almost five years as expectations for another record harvest depress markets as players wait to buy the crop
